arms.predicted: Incremental gain tracking + 0.30s SA restarts will score ≥87.5 consistently and match or exceed iter-2's 87.54 mean, with lower variance due to deeper per-restart exploration.
arms.observed: Three runs scored 87.54, 87.55, 84.82 (mean 86.64, median 87.54). Two fast-machine runs matched iter-2 baseline (87.54-87.55). One slow-machine run dropped to 84.82. Incremental gain + long SA does NOT improve over iter-2's non-incremental SA (87.52-87.57), and does NOT reduce machine-speed variance.
arms.diagnostic_note: h-main matches iter-2 baseline on fast machines but shows no improvement. The incremental gain speedup (more iterations/second) is offset by fewer restarts (3 vs 9). The deeper exploration per restart does not find better optima — suggesting the Max-Cut landscape has many near-equivalent local optima accessible via shallow search.

arms.predicted: Short SA (0.03s per restart, ~30 restarts) with incremental gain tracking will score lower and with higher variance than h-main, because shallow restarts cannot escape deep local optima.
arms.observed: Three runs scored 87.57, 87.57, 84.69 (mean 86.61, median 87.57). On fast-machine runs, h-ablation scored 87.57 — matching or slightly exceeding h-main (87.54-87.55). The slow-machine run (84.69) is comparable to h-main's slow run (84.82). Variance is NOT higher than h-main.
arms.diagnostic_note: Short SA with many restarts performs at parity with long SA with few restarts. This refutes the depth-over-breadth hypothesis: for Max-Cut (n≤1000), random restart diversity is at least as valuable as deep per-restart exploration. The 30 short restarts find the same quality optima as 3 long restarts.

discrepancy_analysis: The core finding is that restart budget allocation (depth vs breadth) does not significantly affect Max-Cut score when using incremental gain tracking. Both h-main (0.30s×3 restarts) and h-ablation (0.03s×30 restarts) score ~87.5 on fast machines, matching iter-2's non-incremental SA. The incremental gain optimization increases per-second iteration count (~5x) but does not translate to higher scores — the bottleneck is not iteration speed but the quality landscape. The dominant variance source remains judge machine speed (bimodal: ~84-85 vs ~87.5), not algorithmic configuration. Both arms' incremental-gain implementations are functionally correct (validated by matching iter-2 scores on fast runs), but neither exceeds the iter-2 ceiling.
